opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that it shouldn't really matter to you, as a developer, where the agent is running. You should be able to think of Codex as one teammate that can work alongside you wherever you are.

Locally, in your terminal or your IDE, it's very interactive. You're pairing with it. You're in the flow, you're asking it to explain a piece of code, make a quick change, run the tests, and you're watching what it does and steering it in real time. That tight loop is really valuable, especially when you're exploring or you're not quite sure yet what you want.

Then there's the remote side, where Codex runs in its own sandboxed environment in the cloud. That's where you can hand off work that's more well-defined, or longer-running. You can kick off several tasks in parallel, go to a meeting, come back, and review what it did. It's more like delegating to a colleague than pairing with one.

What we're really working toward is making those two modes feel seamless. You might start something locally, realize it's going to take a while, and push it to the cloud. Or a task finishes remotely and you pull it down to your machine to iterate on the last ten percent yourself. The context, your preferences, how your repo is set up, all of that should carry across, so you're not starting from scratch every time you switch.

Ultimately, the goal is that you just express what you want done, and Codex figures out the best place to do it, whether that's right next to you on your laptop or out in the cloud working in the background. You stay in control, you review the work, but you're no longer bottlenecked on doing every step yourself.

r001.rationale: It describes Codex as “one teammate” who works locally in the terminal or IDE and remotely in a cloud sandbox.

r002.rationale: It compares local use to pairing and remote use to delegating to a colleague, but does not analogize the environments to communicating with the same human through different channels.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that Codex shouldn't really be a place you go. It should be something that's with you wherever you already are, and the local and remote pieces are two sides of the same agent.

Locally, you've got the CLI and the IDE integration, and that's where you want tight, interactive collaboration. You're in the editor, you have a half-formed idea, you want to point at a function and say "refactor this" or "why does this test fail," and you want the agent working in your actual environment, with your dependencies, your branch, your running dev server. Latency matters there. You're pairing with it.

Remotely, in the cloud, the character of the work changes. You delegate. You hand off a task, or ten tasks, and each one runs in its own sandboxed container with the repo checked out, tests running, and the agent iterating for however long it needs. You come back and there's a pull request waiting with a diff and an explanation of what it did. That's the "fire off a bunch of things and check back later" mode, and it unlocks parallelism that just isn't possible when everything has to go through your laptop and your attention.

The thing we care most about is that those two shouldn't feel like separate products. It should be the same agent, the same underlying model and the same understanding of your codebase, whether it's sitting next to you in the terminal or running in the background on a server. So you might start a task locally, realize it's bigger than you thought, and just push it to the cloud to keep going. Or the reverse: a cloud task comes back with a PR, you pull it down, and you continue iterating locally with the full context of what the agent already tried. Your ChatGPT account, your configuration, your AGENTS.md instructions, all of that travels with you.

Longer term, I think the distinction fades even more. The developer just expresses intent, and the system decides where the work should happen. Quick interactive edits stay close to you. Long-running, well-specified tasks go off and run on their own. You stop thinking about "local versus remote" and start thinking about how many things you can have in flight at once, and how you review and steer them. That's really the shift: from writing code to directing agents that write code, and the environment question becomes an implementation detail that the tooling handles for you.

r001.rationale: The response describes Codex as the same agent working both in the user’s local environment and in remote cloud sandboxes.

r002.rationale: It presents Codex as the same agent across local and remote settings, but does not compare those settings to collaborating with the same human through different communication channels.

astra-6.text:
I think local and remote environments are complementary. Locally, you have this really tight loop: you’re working with Codex, looking at the code, trying something, and giving feedback. That’s useful when you’re still figuring out what you want to build.

Remote environments let you delegate. You can hand off a well-defined task and let it make progress while you focus on something else, then come back and review the result.

The experience I’d like is for those to feel connected. You might start something locally, send it to a remote environment for a longer run, and then bring it back to inspect and refine. The important part is preserving the context across those transitions, so you don’t have to explain the task again every time. You stay in the loop, but you can choose how closely you want to work with the agent at each stage.

r001.rationale: The response describes connected local and remote Codex work, but does not communicate that the remote computing resources belong to Codex.

r002.rationale: It describes moving work between environments, but does not compare that experience to collaborating with the same person through different communication channels.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of local and remote as complementary. Locally, you have the environment you’re already working in, and you can collaborate with Codex in a tight loop: try something, inspect the change, give feedback. Remotely, you can hand off work that can run independently while you focus on something else.

The experience should make it easy to move between those modes. You might start a task locally, send it to a remote environment to keep working, then bring the changes back to review and test. Ideally, the context follows the task, so you don’t have to explain everything again. It feels like one collaborator that can work wherever makes the most sense.

r001.rationale: The response presents Codex as one collaborator working locally and remotely, but does not communicate that the remote computing resources belong to Codex.

r002.rationale: It calls Codex one collaborator across environments, but does not compare that experience to collaborating with the same human through different communication channels.
